text: What process lets green plants use light to make food?
answers: Photosynthesis
Hydroponics
Phytoremediation
Aquaponics
solution: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water. The other terms describe growing systems or cleanup.
hint: Choose the food-making process, rather than a growing location.

text: Which energy arrow best represents photosynthesis?
answers: Light energy → chemical energy in sugar
Chemical energy in soil → light energy
Light energy → mineral nutrients
Oxygen energy → sunlight
solution: Photosynthesis transforms light energy into chemical energy stored in food. It does not turn sunlight into minerals.
hint: Identify the energy source and the form stored in food.

text: A leaf receives sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. What food can it make?
answers: Sugar
Soil
Fish waste
Mineral fertilizer
solution: The plant makes sugar through photosynthesis. Soil and fertilizer can provide support or nutrients, but they are not the food produced.
hint: Plant food and mineral fertilizer are different things.

text: A teammate calls sunlight a kind of plant food. Which correction is most accurate?
answers: Light supplies energy used to make sugar; sugar is food
Light is the sugar already present in the air that leaves absorb
Sunlight supplies minerals directly, so no food-making process is needed
Leaves store the light unchanged as a material instead of making sugar
solution: Sunlight supplies energy, while the plant makes sugar as food. This keeps energy sources separate from substances made by the plant.
hint: Separate the energy used in a process from its food product.

text: How does photosynthesis differ from hydroponics?
answers: One is a food-making process; the other is growing without soil
Both are names for removing pollutants
Only hydroponic plants can make sugar
Photosynthesis requires soil, while hydroponics prevents food making
solution: A plant can photosynthesize while growing hydroponically. The terms describe different aspects of its life.
hint: A process inside a plant can happen in different growing systems.

text: Two similar plants have water and nutrients. One receives suitable light and one stays dark for a long period. Which explanation best predicts a difference?
answers: The dark plant lacks the light energy needed for photosynthesis
The dark plant can obtain all needed food energy from the mineral solution
Any stored food proves the dark plant can make new sugar indefinitely
The light plant receives more soil food simply because its leaves are brighter
solution: Light is an energy input to photosynthesis. Stored food may support a plant temporarily, so darkness does not mean every plant immediately dies.
hint: Consider the missing input and avoid an instant-death assumption.

text: Why is “plants create energy from nothing” a poor explanation?
answers: They transform incoming light energy into energy stored in food
The energy starts to exist only when carbon dioxide enters the leaf
The plant obtains all food energy by absorbing mineral nutrients
The plant turns matter into newly created energy with no energy input
solution: The energy is transferred and transformed, not created from nothing. Food can store chemical energy before it is eaten.
hint: Trace where the energy came from before it was stored.

text: A greenhouse uses suitable lamps instead of sunshine. What question matters for food making?
answers: Whether the plants receive usable light for photosynthesis
Whether the lamps can be absorbed as minerals
Whether a lamp replaces carbon dioxide and water
Whether lamps make soil into sugar without leaves
solution: Plants need suitable light energy, not necessarily direct outdoor sunshine. Water and carbon dioxide are still needed.
hint: Changing the source of light does not remove the other needs.

text: Which gas from the air is used to make sugar during photosynthesis?
answers: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen as the carbon source
Nitrogen as ready-made sugar
Water vapor as the only ingredient
solution: Carbon dioxide supplies carbon used in making sugar. Oxygen is released during photosynthesis rather than being its carbon source.
hint: Look for the air input named in the lesson.

text: Which pair provides material inputs for photosynthesis?
answers: Carbon dioxide and water
Sugar and oxygen
Light and a royal flag
Soil and glass
solution: Water and carbon dioxide are substances used in food making. Light supplies energy, while sugar and oxygen are products.
hint: Distinguish substances used from energy supplied.

text: Which pair identifies products of photosynthesis?
answers: Sugar and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and fertilizer
Water and sunlight
Sand and minerals
solution: The process produces sugar and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water using light. Energy and matter have different roles.
hint: Read the process from inputs toward outputs.

text: A plant gains mass while its pot loses very little soil. Which explanation is most reasonable?
answers: Much of the new plant matter comes from air and water
All the plant’s added mass must come from mineral particles removed from soil
The added mass is sunlight stored as matter without carbon dioxide or water
A plant gaining mass proves it requires no outside material sources
solution: Plants build much of their matter using carbon dioxide and water. They also require mineral nutrients, but do not gain all their mass by consuming soil.
hint: Trace material sources beyond the potting soil.

text: How are mineral nutrients different from the sugar a plant makes?
answers: Minerals support plant functions; sugar is energy-containing food
Minerals are sunlight stored in a bottle
Sugar enters only through roots as fertilizer
Minerals remove the need for carbon dioxide
solution: Plants need minerals, but minerals are not the sugar produced by photosynthesis. Fertilizer does not replace food making.
hint: Do not use the word nutrient to mean every substance has the same job.

text: Which statement correctly follows oxygen in the lesson’s photosynthesis model?
answers: It is produced and released from leaves
It is the only material that enters roots
It is changed directly into sunlight
It is a mineral supplied by gravel
solution: Oxygen is released as a product of photosynthesis. The lesson distinguishes it from carbon dioxide taken in by the plant.
hint: Compare the two gases’ roles in this specific process.

text: Why can light not be listed as a mineral ingredient in a sugar-making model?
answers: Light is an energy input, while minerals are matter
Minerals are the plant’s main energy supply and light is the food substance
Anything required by a plant must be the same kind of material ingredient
Sugar is produced without matter inputs because light replaces carbon dioxide
solution: The model should distinguish energy entering as light from matter entering as substances. Both are important but not interchangeable.
hint: Ask whether something is energy or a material substance.

text: A hydroponic plant has light and nutrient solution. What must the air still provide for photosynthesis?
answers: Carbon dioxide
Ready-made soil particles
Sugar crystals as the only food source
Fish scales in every system
solution: Hydroponics does not remove the need for carbon dioxide. The plant still makes food using the normal photosynthesis inputs.
hint: A different growing medium does not change the basic food-making process.

text: Which plant structures mainly absorb water from the growing environment?
answers: Roots
Flowers
Fruits
Seeds stored in a packet
solution: Roots absorb water and dissolved mineral nutrients. Other structures have different functions in the plant.
hint: Start tracing water at the part in contact with the water supply.

text: Which simplified route traces water toward food-making leaves?
answers: Roots → stems → leaves
Leaves → fruit → sunlight
Stems → soil → air
Flowers → compass → roots
solution: Water absorbed by roots is transported through stems toward leaves. This is a material pathway, not an energy transformation.
hint: Follow water from its entry point to the leaves.

text: Where does carbon dioxide enter a leaf in the supplied explanation?
answers: Through openings in the leaf
Through seeds being eaten by animals
Only through mineral grains in soil
Only through the flower’s colored petals
solution: Carbon dioxide enters through leaf openings. Water normally follows a different path through roots and stems.
hint: Compare the gas pathway with the water pathway.

text: A diagram shows roots absorbing sunshine and leaves taking in soil. Which revision is strongest?
answers: Show roots absorbing water and leaves absorbing light and taking in carbon dioxide
Show roots taking in ready-made sugar from every soil and leaves only releasing gases
Keep the root arrow as light because roots supply all energy to the leaves
Show minerals entering the leaves as the only source of plant food energy
solution: The corrected model assigns different functions to structures. Leaves and roots do not obtain the same inputs in the same way.
hint: Match each structure with the input it actually helps obtain.

text: How do roots and stems cooperate in the water pathway?
answers: Roots take in water; stems help transport it
Stems make soil; roots turn it into sunlight
Both only produce seeds
Roots supply light while stems supply carbon dioxide from soil
solution: Absorption and transport are connected but distinct jobs. Water must reach the parts using it after entering through roots.
hint: Separate getting water into the plant from moving it inside.

text: A plant has healthy roots but most leaves are removed. Which concern directly relates to photosynthesis?
answers: There is less leaf area available to absorb light
The roots will automatically replace all the leaves’ light-absorbing work
Stored food means the plant will never need to make any new sugar
The remaining growing medium will now supply every bit of food energy
solution: Leaves help capture light for photosynthesis. Stored resources and remaining tissues matter too, so an immediate universal outcome is not established.
hint: Focus on the affected structure’s role without exaggerating the consequence.

text: Why can a support material alone not do the job of roots?
answers: Holding a plant upright is different from absorbing water and nutrients
A support material automatically supplies water even when no water is present
Any material holding roots provides all the mineral nutrients the plant needs
The only purpose of roots is support, so a nonliving medium does every root job
solution: A medium can hold roots in place, while roots still need access to water and nutrients. Physical support and absorption are different functions.
hint: Distinguish the medium’s role from the living structure’s role.

text: Which structure is directly involved in both taking in carbon dioxide and releasing photosynthesis oxygen?
answers: Leaf openings
A bottle’s foil cover
The seed packet
A gravel support layer
solution: Leaf openings allow gas exchange. Equipment in a growing system can support conditions but does not replace living structures.
hint: Look for the structure on the plant rather than the equipment around it.

text: Why are green plants called producers?
answers: They make their own food
They eat only fruit
They make all their minerals from sunlight
They must consume animals for energy
solution: Producers make food rather than obtaining all their food by eating other organisms. Green plants use photosynthesis to do this.
hint: Use the food-making meaning of producer.

text: Which path follows food energy to a person eating an apple?
answers: Sunlight → apple tree’s food → person
Soil minerals → sunlight → person
Person → apple → the sun
Water bottle → fish tank → sunlight
solution: The tree captures light energy and stores chemical energy in food. Eating the apple transfers some of that food energy to the consumer.
hint: Trace the original source before the food is eaten.

text: A caterpillar eats a green leaf. Which pairing is correct?
answers: Plant: producer; caterpillar: consumer
Plant: consumer; caterpillar: producer
Both are producers because both grow
Both make sugar directly from sunlight
solution: The plant makes food, while the caterpillar obtains food by eating. Growth alone does not make an organism a producer.
hint: Classify by how food is obtained, not whether the organism grows.

text: A teammate says an apple tree becomes a consumer when roots absorb minerals. Which correction is strongest?
answers: Absorbing minerals does not mean eating food; the tree still produces sugar
Taking in water or minerals is the same as eating ready-made food
Only plants rooted in soil can be called producers, regardless of food making
Producing sugar removes any need for materials from the surrounding environment
solution: Mineral uptake and food making are distinct. A plant remains a producer even though it obtains materials from its surroundings.
hint: Do not equate every absorbed substance with eating food.

text: A lettuce plant grows in nutrient solution instead of soil. Does its producer role change?
answers: No; it can still make food using light
Yes; water makes it a fish
Yes; nutrient solution prevents photosynthesis
No; producers never need any materials
solution: Growing location does not decide the role. A green lettuce plant can photosynthesize in a properly supplied hydroponic system.
hint: Classify by food making rather than the growing medium.

text: Which evidence most directly supports calling a green plant a producer?
answers: It makes sugar from carbon dioxide and water using light
Its roots absorb mineral nutrients from the water around them
It grows taller after receiving a suitable amount of fertilizer
It has green leaves and was placed in a bright growing area
solution: The defining evidence concerns food production. Size, color of equipment, and where it was bought do not establish the ecological role.
hint: Choose evidence that directly addresses the definition.

text: Why is a plant-eating animal a consumer even though its food was once made using sunlight?
answers: It obtains the food by eating rather than making it by photosynthesis
Receiving energy that originated in sunlight makes every eater a producer
The animal’s body converts the eaten leaf directly into new incoming sunlight
The animal gets its food energy chiefly from minerals it absorbs with the leaf
solution: The original energy source does not make every organism along the pathway a producer. How it obtains food matters.
hint: Distinguish where energy originated from how this organism gets food.

text: Which set is correctly classified?
answers: Corn plant: producer; corn-eating person: consumer
Corn plant: consumer; corn-eating person: producer
Corn plant and person: both hydroponics systems
Corn plant and person: both make all food from air
solution: The corn plant produces food and the eater consumes plant products. Their roles differ even though energy passes between them.
hint: Follow the food-making and food-eating actions.

text: In what form is energy stored in the sugar a plant makes?
answers: Chemical energy
Only sound energy
Only gravitational energy
A mineral called sunlight
solution: The lesson describes light energy transformed into chemical energy stored in sugar. That food can later support life processes.
hint: Name the stored form rather than the incoming source.

text: Which group lists uses of food energy by a plant?
answers: Growth, repair, and reproduction
Only feeding humans and never the plant
Only holding the pot upright
Replacing every need for water and air
solution: Plants use food energy for their own life processes, including growth, repair, and reproduction. They do not make food solely for people.
hint: Look for activities of the living plant itself.

text: A person eats corn. What happens to energy stored in the corn?
answers: Some food energy becomes available to the person
All the energy turns back into sunlight before eating
The energy is created for the first time in the mouth
Only the corn’s support pot transfers energy
solution: Eating plant products can pass chemical energy to a consumer. The energy was already stored before the food was eaten.
hint: Keep the energy pathway continuous rather than inventing a new source.

text: Which correction addresses “plants make food only for animals”?
answers: Plants also use their food for their own growth, repair, and reproduction
The plant needs minerals but never uses the sugar that its leaves make
Stored food matters only for animals, while plant growth requires no energy
Only seeds use food energy; an established plant uses water instead of food
solution: Plants are living organisms with their own energy needs. Consumers may later obtain some energy by eating plants or plant products.
hint: Consider the plant’s needs before considering its eaters.

text: Which pairing correctly distinguishes storage and use?
answers: Sugar stores chemical energy; growth is one use of food energy
A rock stores sunlight as fertilizer; roots use it as a compass
A seed packet makes sugar; a pot reproduces
Water is always the only food energy store
solution: Food can store chemical energy, and life processes use it. A growing system’s nonliving equipment has different roles.
hint: Separate an energy-containing substance from a process requiring energy.

text: A plant remains alive briefly after being put in darkness. What should that observation NOT be used to prove?
answers: That plants never need light to make food
The plant may have used food stored before it was placed in darkness
A brief observation does not establish every long-term growth condition
A plant can remain alive for some time without making new food
solution: Stored food can support a plant temporarily. A short observation does not refute the role of light in photosynthesis.
hint: Compare temporary survival with continued food production.

text: Why can energy in an apple be traced back to sunlight?
answers: The tree used light energy while making food that stores chemical energy
The apple’s energy comes chiefly from mineral nutrients absorbed from soil
The apple creates its own energy after it has separated from the tree
The eater creates all the food energy only when the apple is consumed
solution: The plant’s photosynthesis connects light energy with stored food energy. The consumer receives energy that already had a source.
hint: Trace backward from food to the process that made it.

text: A model of food energy should include which connection?
answers: Plant food can support the plant and also pass energy to an eater
Only animals need energy, so plants have no uses for food
Food changes into a producer as soon as it is eaten
Sunlight removes every need for material inputs
solution: The model should represent both plant uses and transfer to consumers. Matter inputs remain needed during food making.
hint: Include the producer’s life processes as well as the consumer’s meal.

text: What is hydroponics?
answers: Growing plants without soil using a supplied nutrient solution
Using plants only to clean a polluted field
Raising fish with no plants
A process that turns sunlight into a mineral
solution: Hydroponics supplies water and dissolved mineral nutrients without soil. Plants still need light and air to make food.
hint: The term describes a growing method, not a different photosynthesis process.

text: In a hydroponic system, what can nutrient-free rocks provide?
answers: Physical support for roots
All the sugar the plant will ever need
A replacement for every mineral nutrient
A way to remove the need for light
solution: A growing medium may support roots without supplying nutrients. The nutrient solution serves a different role.
hint: Separate support from dissolved nutrient supply.

text: A gardener has a small sunny patio and little soil space. Why might hydroponics be useful?
answers: It can grow plants in a managed system without a soil bed
It guarantees growth without water or nutrients
It works only on very large farms
It means the plants no longer need suitable light
solution: The photos describe use in small spaces as well as larger farms. Hydroponics changes the growing setup, not all the plants’ needs.
hint: Match the method’s useful feature to the available space.

text: A teammate interprets “no soil” as “plain water supplies every long-term need.” Which correction is best?
answers: Mineral nutrients still need to be supplied, along with other suitable conditions
Every plain-water supply contains a complete, suitable mineral balance
The support medium always supplies every mineral even if it contains none
Light supplies all the minerals that are missing from the water
solution: Soil is not essential as a medium, but mineral nutrients remain necessary. Nutrient-rich water is an important part of the supplied growing method.
hint: Removing soil does not remove the need for minerals.

text: Which distinction explains soil-based and hydroponic growing?
answers: Hydroponics supplies nutrients without requiring soil as the medium
Soil-based plants never photosynthesize
Hydroponic plants must get all their energy from fertilizer
Hydroponics is defined only by whether the container is indoors
solution: Both can support photosynthesizing plants. The key distinction is the growing medium and nutrient delivery, not whether food making occurs.
hint: Compare methods of growing, not different kinds of food-making chemistry.

text: A lettuce plant grows for weeks in a soil-free system supplied with nutrients, water, air, and light. What does this support?
answers: Soil itself is not required when the plant’s needs are met
Any plant can now grow for the same time with all of those inputs removed
The observed growth proves pure water alone provides every long-term need
The result proves mineral nutrients supply all the plant’s food energy
solution: The result supports soil-free growth under those conditions. It does not justify dropping the supplied nutrients or other inputs.
hint: Keep all the conditions of the observation in your claim.

text: Why does “fertilizer is plant food” risk confusing this lesson’s model?
answers: Fertilizer supplies mineral nutrients; the plant makes sugar using light
Fertilizer provides the energy in sugar directly, so light is only for warmth
Minerals and sugars have the same role because both can enter a growing system
A hydroponic plant obtains ready-made sugar from any nutrient solution
solution: The distinction keeps mineral supply separate from photosynthesis and chemical energy in sugar. Both processes contribute to plant health.
hint: Clarify the different jobs rather than treating all inputs as food.

text: Which setup best matches the supplied hydroponics description?
answers: Roots supported above nutrient-rich water with access through a wick
Roots kept dry inside a sealed dark container
A pot containing only plastic leaves and dry rocks
A fish tank that contains no plant and no growing area
solution: The setup supplies water and minerals to living plants without soil. Support and access to the solution are both relevant.
hint: Look for a plant, no soil requirement, and a path to nutrient solution.

text: What combination is central to aquaponics?
answers: Raising aquatic animals together with hydroponic plant growing
Only growing plants in dry soil
Only using sunlight to clean a rock
Only collecting rainwater with no organisms
solution: Aquaponics links aquatic-animal care with soil-free plant growing. The linked system cycles water and can use waste-derived nutrients.
hint: Look for both an aquatic-animal part and a plant-growing part.

text: Which simplified path fits the aquaponics reading?
answers: Water from the aquatic-animal area → plant-growing area → back through the system
Sunlight → fish scales → soil-only planting
Plants → dry gravel → no returning water
Fish tank → ocean → no plant-growing area
solution: The supplied model circulates water between aquatic animals and hydroponic plants. It is not just two unrelated containers.
hint: Follow the water connection between the two parts.

text: What can fish waste contribute to the linked plant-growing system?
answers: A source of nutrients through processes in the water system
All the light energy needed for photosynthesis
A guarantee that no monitoring is needed
A replacement for carbon dioxide in making sugar
solution: Waste-derived substances can supply plant nutrients through system processes. They do not replace light energy or every other plant need.
hint: Distinguish mineral supply from the source of food energy.

text: A teammate says aquaponic plants get all their sugar directly from fish waste. Which correction is strongest?
answers: They still make sugar using light, carbon dioxide, and water
Waste-derived mineral nutrients are identical to the sugar plants make
The connected water route removes the plant’s need for carbon dioxide
Plant roots get all food energy directly from the fish rather than light
solution: The system can supply nutrients while plants still photosynthesize. Nutrient sources and food making are different parts of the explanation.
hint: Use the same food-making model for a different growing setup.

text: What additional living component distinguishes aquaponics from a plant-only hydroponic system?
answers: Aquatic animals such as fish
A requirement for ordinary garden soil
A rule that no plant receives light
Only an empty container of water
solution: Aquaponics includes an aquatic-animal component linked with plant growing. Hydroponics alone does not require fish.
hint: Identify what is added to the plant-growing method.

text: Why is placing one fish beside one potted plant not enough to demonstrate aquaponics?
answers: The nutrient and water connection between the parts must be shown
Putting containers nearby guarantees a nutrient flow even without a water link
Having a fish and a plant in one photo is enough to prove a managed system
Any potted plant beside a fish tank must obtain nutrients from that tank
solution: Aquaponics describes a linked growing system, not mere proximity. Evidence should show how water and nutrient flows connect its parts.
hint: Look for functional connections rather than just two labels.

text: Which explanation keeps matter and energy distinct in aquaponics?
answers: Waste-derived nutrients can move through water while light powers plant food making
Nutrients in fish waste are the plant’s main replacement for light energy
Recirculating water removes the need for any incoming energy to make food
The water’s movement creates the sugar directly, without photosynthesis
solution: Matter can circulate through the system, while the plant’s light input has a separate role. A pump’s movement is not photosynthesis.
hint: Trace a material pathway and an energy source separately.

text: Which observation would best show that the two parts of an aquaponic model are connected?
answers: Water is directed from the animal area through the plant area and recirculated
Both containers are painted the same color
Both labels have the word science on them
The fish tank is photographed near a seed packet
solution: A visible water route supports the claimed connection. Appearance alone does not establish nutrient or water transfer.
hint: Choose evidence about the system’s working pathway.

text: What is an epiphyte in the supplied lesson?
answers: A plant that grows on another plant for support
Any animal that eats tree leaves
A plant that can live without water indefinitely
A mineral that dissolves in a fish tank
solution: Epiphytes use other plants as growing places. They still need water, nutrients, light, and air for their own life processes.
hint: Focus on the growing location without removing the plant’s basic needs.

text: Which sources can supply an epiphyte with water and nutrients?
answers: Rain and material reaching it from the surrounding environment
Only sugar stolen from every supporting tree
Only nutrients produced from sunshine
Only deep soil directly around every root
solution: The lesson emphasizes air and rain; debris and deposited material can supply nutrients. Support does not necessarily mean drawing food from the host.
hint: Separate environmental supplies from the structure providing support.

text: An orchid grows on a branch and makes sugar in its green leaves. Which explanation fits?
answers: The branch can provide support while the orchid makes its own food
The orchid must be a consumer because it touches a tree
The branch replaces the orchid’s need for sunlight
Every orchid always grows only on branches
solution: The example fits an epiphytic growing habit. It does not establish that every orchid has that habit or that the plant eats its support.
hint: Distinguish this example from an unsupported claim about every orchid.

text: A teammate says any plant growing on a tree must steal the tree’s food. What is the best response?
answers: Some are epiphytes using the tree as support while making their own food
Every attachment to a branch proves the growing plant takes sugar from that tree
Any plant growing above soil can receive all its energy from the supporting bark
A branch provides all water and minerals automatically without other sources
solution: The epiphyte example shows why growing location alone does not establish parasitism. Different tree-growing plants can have different relationships.
hint: A location is not enough evidence to establish how food is obtained.

text: What do a green epiphyte and a green hydroponic lettuce plant have in common?
answers: Both can make food without growing in ordinary soil
Neither needs water or minerals
Both must obtain every nutrient from fish
Neither needs carbon dioxide
solution: Both illustrate alternatives to ordinary soil growing. Their water and nutrient sources may differ while their photosynthesis needs remain.
hint: Look for a shared growing feature without dropping basic needs.

text: A researcher observes one bromeliad growing on a tree. Which conclusion exceeds that evidence?
answers: Every bromeliad must grow only on trees
The observed bromeliad uses the branch as one growing location
This example could be investigated as a possible epiphyte
Further observations could help identify this plant’s water supply
solution: One example cannot establish the habits of every member of a group. The lesson gives examples, not universal rules for all orchids, mosses, or bromeliads.
hint: Watch for an “every” claim based on a single observation.

text: Why is the nickname air plant not evidence that a plant needs no water?
answers: The plant can receive water from rain or moisture in its surroundings
A soil-free location guarantees water is never needed for growth
Any plant with the word air in its name receives food energy from minerals
A common name is enough evidence to replace observations of plant needs
solution: Common names are not complete explanations of needs. The supplied reading explicitly connects these plants with water from their environment.
hint: Use the described sources rather than interpreting a nickname literally.

text: Which example best illustrates support without soil in this lesson?
answers: An epiphytic plant attached to a tree branch
A plant making all its food by consuming a branch
A seed packet stored on a shelf without a living plant
A leaf that turns every mineral into sunlight
solution: The branch supplies a growing place, while the epiphyte obtains its supplies and makes food. It is a living-plant example rather than stored equipment.
hint: Identify a living plant’s support relationship.

text: What does phytoremediation use to help clean contaminated places?
answers: Plants
Only magnetic compasses
Only seed-packet labels
Only ordinary plastic pots
solution: Phytoremediation uses plants to help manage pollutants. Which plants and methods work depends on the contaminant and conditions.
hint: The word refers to a plant-based cleanup method.

text: Which pathway fits the cleanup example in the reading?
answers: A plant takes up some pollutants and stores them in its tissues
Sunlight removes all matter from the site instantly
A container label turns every pollutant into water
Minerals stop every plant from growing
solution: Some plants can take up and store pollutants; some processes can transform certain contaminants. This is not instant universal removal.
hint: Trace where a contaminant could go instead of assuming it vanishes.

text: Why are sunflowers mentioned in the cleanup section?
answers: As an example of plants used in phytoremediation
As proof that every sunflower makes any soil harmless
As plants that never need mineral nutrients
As organisms that make food without light
solution: The sunflower is an example within a cleanup method. An example does not prove all plants treat all pollutants under all conditions.
hint: Keep an example separate from a universal guarantee.

text: A teammate says planting flowers guarantees every polluted site is safe the next day. Which correction is strongest?
answers: Effectiveness depends on the pollutant, plant, conditions, and time
A healthy-looking flower alone proves all target pollutants have been removed
The name of the method establishes that any plant will treat any contaminant
Planting sunflowers guarantees identical results regardless of conditions
solution: Plant-based cleanup has limits and must be evaluated. The lesson’s general example is not a guarantee for every site.
hint: Look for evidence and conditions rather than an absolute claim.

text: How does phytoremediation differ from hydroponics?
answers: One concerns cleanup using plants; the other concerns growing without soil
Both names mean raising fish only
Hydroponics always requires polluted water
Phytoremediation means every plant is grown in gravel
solution: These terms describe different purposes or methods. A question about cleanup is different from one about soil-free nutrient delivery.
hint: Identify the purpose addressed by each term.

text: Which observation is most relevant to evaluating a plant-based water treatment?
answers: Measurements show the target pollutant decreases under the tested conditions
The treated plants grew taller, but the pollutant was not measured
The water appeared clearer, without checking the target pollutant
A different pollutant decreased in a different site with different conditions
solution: Measurements tied to the target pollutant directly address cleanup. Names and appearances alone do not establish treatment effectiveness.
hint: Choose evidence that measures the claim being made.

text: If a pollutant is stored in roots, why is “the pollutant no longer exists” an incorrect conclusion?
answers: Storage in tissue changes its location, not necessarily its identity
Any material entering a root has necessarily been changed into a harmless substance
A pollutant absorbed by a plant has necessarily ceased to be matter
Healthy-looking plant tissue proves that every stored contaminant is harmless
solution: Taking up a material is not the same as destroying it. Some contaminants may be transformed, but that requires relevant evidence.
hint: Distinguish moving a substance from changing or eliminating it.

text: Which question should scientists ask before claiming a plant treatment worked?
answers: What pollutant was measured, and how did its amount change?
Was the plant’s name written in green ink?
Did the container have a science sticker?
Was a sunflower mentioned anywhere in the report?
solution: A supported claim identifies the target material and the evidence of change. A familiar plant example is not enough by itself.
hint: Connect the claim with a measured before-and-after comparison.

text: What is the main job of the cloth wick in the bottle activity?
answers: Providing a path for water to reach the growing medium
Making sunlight inside the bottle
Creating every mineral from nothing
Turning the seeds into fertilizer
solution: The cloth connects the water supply below with the growing area above. It helps move water rather than making food or minerals.
hint: Trace the physical connection between reservoir and growing area.

text: What is the role of the growing medium in the supplied bottle system?
answers: Supporting the seeds and roots
Replacing all need for water
Guaranteeing every nutrient without a solution
Taking the place of light for photosynthesis
solution: The medium provides support; the solution supplies water and added minerals. The roles should not be treated as identical.
hint: Compare physical support with the substances dissolved in water.

text: How should the amount of fertilizer be chosen for the activity?
answers: Follow the product label for the stated water amount
Use the same large scoop for every product
Double the dose whenever the bottle is smaller
Replace all water with dry fertilizer
solution: The photographed directions refer to the fertilizer label. They do not provide one universal dose suitable for every formulation.
hint: Use the source of dosing directions named in the activity.

text: To compare nutrient solution with plain water, which plan is fairest?
answers: Keep plant type, light, water access, and time comparable while changing nutrient supply
Use different plant species because that makes nutrient effects easier to isolate
Give one group more light and more nutrients to identify the effect of nutrients alone
Compare unequal observation periods without recording the difference
solution: Changing several conditions at once makes it harder to explain a difference. A planned comparison isolates the chosen factor as well as practical conditions allow.
hint: Change the factor being studied and control other important conditions.

text: Which source tells the student how deep to plant the seeds in the pictured activity?
answers: The seed packet’s directions
The bottle’s color alone
The fish’s size
The name of the sunniest room
solution: The activity directs the student to the seed packet for planting depth. Different seeds can have different instructions.
hint: Choose a source with information about the particular seeds.

text: One seedling droops in a bottle system. What is the strongest next step?
answers: Check water access, light, nutrients, and observations before assigning one cause
Add more fertilizer immediately because drooping always identifies a nutrient shortage
Declare the medium unsuitable without checking the water route or other conditions
Conclude one seedling proves every hydroponic setup will have the same outcome
solution: A symptom can have more than one cause. Checking conditions and collecting evidence is stronger than making a single confident diagnosis.
hint: An observation can guide investigation without identifying one certain cause.

text: Why should the wick reach the reservoir rather than stop above the water?
answers: It needs contact with the water supply to provide the intended path
A dry wick disconnected from the reservoir can provide the same water access
The wick only supplies minerals, so contact with any water is irrelevant
The growing medium will always move reservoir water across an empty air gap
solution: The designed pathway depends on contact between the water supply and the wick. A disconnected component does not provide the intended transfer.
hint: Check whether the parts form a continuous working connection.

text: Which record would best support a comparison of two growing conditions?
answers: Repeated observations of similar plants over the same period
Only the names given to the bottles
Only the color of each label
One picture taken before either group is planted
solution: Comparable repeated observations give evidence about growth. Labels and a single pre-planting photo do not establish outcomes.
hint: Record results related to the question over comparable times.

text: A squad inflates a balloon. Which explanation shows why the added air is matter?
answers: It has mass and takes up space
It can only be matter if it is visible
It has no mass because it is a gas
It becomes matter only after it freezes
solution: Air is matter: gases have mass and occupy space. Being invisible does not make air an energy source instead of matter.
hint: Use the two defining properties of matter.

text: Which sentence uses material to mean matter from which something is made?
answers: The chair is made from wood
The chair grew taller yesterday
The chair feels heavy to lift
The chair stands beside a window
solution: Wood is a material because it is matter used to make the chair. Growth describes change, and weight describes gravity’s pull.
hint: Ask what the object is made from.

text: Which statement correctly distinguishes a seed’s mass from its weight?
answers: Mass is its amount of matter; weight is gravity’s pull on it
Mass is its height; weight is the number of leaves
Mass is stored light; weight is stored water
Mass and weight both mean the space it takes up
solution: Mass measures the amount of matter. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass. Neither word means the same thing as volume.
hint: One word describes matter; the other describes a force.

text: A growth diagram shows water + sunlight → all new plant matter. Which revision best separates matter from energy?
answers: Add carbon dioxide as matter and show light supplying energy
Replace water with oxygen and show soil supplying all energy
Keep only sunlight because light supplies all new material
Add fertilizer and label sunlight as a mineral
solution: Water and carbon dioxide supply matter for photosynthesis. Light provides energy, not material. The revised model must distinguish these inputs.
hint: Find the missing input from air and check what light supplies.

text: Which label belongs on the arrow from the Sun to a green leaf?
answers: Light energy
Dissolved minerals
Carbon dioxide matter
Stored sugar matter
solution: The Sun supplies light energy for photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide and water are matter inputs; minerals are not light.
hint: Distinguish an energy input from a material input.

text: The squad calls photosynthesis a food-making process. Which change supports that description?
answers: Carbon dioxide and water become sugar using light
Roots turn all absorbed minerals directly into sunlight
Leaves change oxygen into soil using sugar
Water becomes fertilizer without an energy input
solution: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. Sugar is the food product.
hint: Choose the process with the correct matter inputs and food output.

text: A student labels both sugar and sunlight as material ingredients entering a leaf during photosynthesis. What is the best correction?
answers: Light supplies energy; sugar is a product
Light supplies minerals; sugar is an input
Light supplies water; sugar is a gas input
Light supplies soil; sugar is unchanged
solution: The model should show sunlight as an energy input and sugar as a food output. Water and carbon dioxide are the matter inputs.
hint: Separate what enters, what is made, and what powers the change.

text: Which paired description correctly names photosynthesis and its energy change?
answers: Food making; light energy becomes stored chemical energy
Water transport; chemical energy becomes soil
Mineral uptake; roots create light energy
Seed dispersal; air changes into gravity
solution: Photosynthesis makes food, storing captured light energy as chemical energy in sugar. It is different from transport or seed dispersal.
hint: Match the process to making sugar, not merely moving water.

text: A seedling has roots, a stem, and leaves. What word names these parts as features with jobs?
answers: Structures
Consumers
Pollutants
Products
solution: Roots, stems, and leaves are structures. Their different jobs help the plant obtain inputs, transport materials, and make food.
hint: Think of the word for the parts of an organism.

text: A table lists leaves → light and roots → water. What important matter input should be added at leaves?
answers: Carbon dioxide from air
Sugar from the Sun
Soil from the stem
Minerals from sunlight
solution: Leaves capture light and take in carbon dioxide from air. Roots absorb water. Light is energy; carbon dioxide and water supply matter.
hint: Consider the gas needed for food making.

text: Water reaches roots in the bottle lab. Which structure normally carries it toward the leaves?
answers: The stem
The flower petal
The seed coat
The fruit
solution: Stems transport water from roots toward leaves. A model should connect the structures by the material they move.
hint: Trace the route between the roots and leaves.

text: A plant model puts carbon dioxide entering the roots from sunlight. Which replacement is sound?
answers: Carbon dioxide enters leaves from air
Carbon dioxide enters fruit from rocks
Carbon dioxide enters roots from light
Carbon dioxide enters stems as fertilizer
solution: Carbon dioxide is a gas in air that can enter leaf openings. Sunlight is an energy source, not a source of carbon dioxide.
hint: Identify both the correct source and the entry structure.

text: Which observation is the clearest example of seedling growth?
answers: New roots and leaves develop over several days
A leaf blows from one side of a tray to another
A pot is moved from a shelf onto a table
Water is poured from a cup into a bottle
solution: Growth can increase size and complexity. Developing new roots and leaves is growth; relocating a leaf or container is movement.
hint: Look for a change in the organism, not its location.

text: A seed sprouts before it has green leaves. What supplies food for that earliest growth?
answers: Food stored in the seed
Sugar made by the empty bottle
Food created by the growing medium alone
Sunlight stored as a mineral in water
solution: Stored seed food supports early germination. Once green leaves develop, photosynthesis can make more food for continued growth.
hint: A seed contains supplies for its beginning stages.

text: Which sequence best matches a seed developing into a young plant?
answers: Seed takes in water → root emerges → shoot and leaves develop
Mature fruit forms → roots disappear → seed takes in water
Leaves become soil → stem absorbs light → seed grows
Root takes in sunlight → flower becomes water → shoot forms
solution: Seeds take in water during germination, roots emerge, and shoots and leaves develop. This sequence tracks increasing structures through time.
hint: Start with the seed and follow the first new structures.

text: Two seeds sprout in darkness for a short time. Which conclusion goes beyond the evidence?
answers: Green plants never need light for continued growth
Stored food may support early seed growth
Seeds can change before green leaves form
A longer investigation would give more evidence
solution: Short-term sprouting can use stored seed food. It does not show that a green plant can continue making food without light.
hint: Separate an early observation from a claim about the whole life of a plant.

text: Which claim best explains why the green plants in this lesson are producers?
answers: They use light to make their own food
They obtain food by eating smaller plants
They receive ready-made sugar from sunlight
They turn every mineral directly into energy
solution: Producers such as green plants make food through photosynthesis. They do not get ready-made sugar from the Sun or eat soil.
hint: Focus on how they obtain food.

text: A mushroom stays in one place, and a bean plant stays rooted. Is staying in one place enough to show both make food by photosynthesis?
answers: No; food-making process determines producer status
Yes; all organisms that stay still capture sunlight
Yes; movement alone determines food source
No; rooted plants cannot make their own food
solution: Being stationary does not establish how food is obtained. Green plants photosynthesize; a mushroom gets food differently.
hint: Use how food is obtained rather than movement alone.

text: A caterpillar eats a leaf that a green plant grew. Which path traces the original source of its food energy?
answers: Sunlight → plant food → caterpillar
Minerals → sunlight → caterpillar
Caterpillar → leaf → sunlight
Soil → caterpillar → sunlight
solution: Light energy is stored in the plant’s food as chemical energy. Eating the leaf passes some of that stored energy to the caterpillar.
hint: Follow energy from the source to food to the eater.

text: No animal visits a greenhouse for a week. Do its green plants stop being producers?
answers: No; they can still make their own food
Yes; a producer must be eaten each day
Yes; without animals they become consumers
No; producers obtain all food from soil
solution: Producer describes food making, not how often an organism is eaten. The plants can photosynthesize when their needs are met.
hint: A role is based on obtaining food, not having visitors.

text: A soil-free seedling forms leaves in nutrient water. Which claim matches this observation without overstating it?
answers: Plants can grow without soil when their needs are met
Plants never need minerals or carbon dioxide
Water supplies every need for every plant forever
Light supplies all the matter in new leaves
solution: The observation supports soil-free growth under suitable conditions. Air, water, light energy, nutrients, and seed reserves must be considered.
hint: State what the observation supports, without claiming all needs disappeared.

text: Which description best identifies hydroponics in a field guide?
answers: Growing plants without soil using a nutrient-water supply
Growing plants on branches using only host-tree sugar
Growing plants only in outdoor soil beds
Using plants only to measure air temperature
solution: Hydroponics is soil-free growing with a supply of dissolved nutrients in water. It is not defined by location or by growing on a tree.
hint: Identify the growing method, not just whether it is indoors.

text: A seed sprouts on a wet paper towel with no added minerals. What is the most careful interpretation?
answers: Early seed reserves do not prove plain water meets every long-term need
The seed proves that minerals never matter to plants
The paper must have supplied all future plant food
The water must have turned into sunlight
solution: Early seed growth can draw on stored supplies. Continued healthy growth still requires suitable conditions and mineral nutrients.
hint: Distinguish a brief germination trial from long-term growth.

text: A squad removes soil but keeps light, air, nutrient water, and root support. Which question is this setup most directly designed to explore?
answers: Can plants grow when soil is absent but other needs are met?
Can plants grow without any source of matter?
Can plants make food with no energy supply?
Can plants grow without water or air?
solution: The setup removes soil while retaining other supplies. It explores whether soil itself is necessary, not whether matter or energy is unnecessary.
hint: Name the condition removed and notice what stays available.

text: Which pair of parts belongs in an aquaponics overview diagram?
answers: Aquatic animals and hydroponic plants
Only dry seeds and sealed empty bottles
Only tree branches and epiphytes
Only polluted soil and sunflowers
solution: Aquaponics links raising aquatic animals with hydroponic growing. Its water and nutrient flows connect the animal and plant parts.
hint: The name combines aquatic animals with a soil-free growing system.

text: A diagram shows fish waste supplying plant nutrients but leaves out light. What should a science explanation add?
answers: Plants still need light energy to make sugar
Fish waste replaces every need for light
Roots create sunlight from fish food
Fish make all the sugar for plant leaves
solution: Fish-linked waste can supply mineral nutrients through the system. Plants still use light energy for photosynthesis and make their own sugar.
hint: Nutrients and the energy used to make food are different supplies.

text: Which feature distinguishes an aquaponic system from a hydroponic system without animals?
answers: An aquatic-animal component is linked to plant growing
All water must stay still permanently
Neither system needs mineral nutrients
Only aquaponics uses photosynthesis
solution: Aquaponics adds a linked aquatic-animal component. Both approaches can grow plants in nutrient water, and green plants in both photosynthesize.
hint: Compare the components rather than changing how leaves make food.

text: Why is a circular water arrow useful in an aquaponics model?
answers: It represents water moving between linked system parts
It means water creates energy without light
It proves no maintenance is ever needed
It means nutrients disappear before reaching plants
solution: A circular arrow models water circulation among connected parts. It does not prove that the system manages itself or supplies energy without light.
hint: Explain what the arrow represents without adding unsupported claims.

text: Which description belongs beside epiphyte in a vocabulary guide?
answers: A plant growing on another plant for support
A plant that must get all sugar from its host
A fish raised together with root vegetables
A mineral added to hydroponic water
solution: An epiphyte grows on another plant as support. Green epiphytes can make their own food rather than necessarily taking the host’s sugar.
hint: Separate a place to grow from a food supply.

text: A green epiphyte receives rain but no host-tree sugar. Which source can still provide its food?
answers: Its own photosynthesis
Its branch turning into ready-made sugar
The air replacing all need for light
The host’s bark automatically becoming its roots
solution: A green epiphyte uses light energy, carbon dioxide, and water to make sugar. The host can serve as support without supplying food.
hint: Recall what a green plant can make in its leaves.

text: A guide says every plant found on a tree steals the tree’s food. Which evidence would challenge that generalization?
answers: An epiphyte uses the tree for support and makes its own sugar
The epiphyte takes sugar directly from the host’s tissues
The epiphyte cannot make sugar and relies on host food
The host supplies both support and all of the epiphyte’s food
solution: Evidence of support without taking host food challenges the claim. Location alone does not show whether a plant is a parasite.
hint: Choose evidence about the food source, not just appearance.

text: Which supply pairing correctly describes a green epiphyte?
answers: Branch: support; sunlight: energy for food making
Branch: sunlight; rain: all ready-made food
Air: no matter; branch: all sugar
Sunlight: mineral nutrients; rain: support only
solution: The branch provides physical support and sunlight supplies energy. Rain and surrounding material can provide water and nutrients.
hint: Match each source to the role it really plays.

text: A field guide defines phytoremediation. Which wording is most accurate?
answers: Using plants to help treat certain pollutants
Growing every plant without any water
Growing fish without a nutrient cycle
Turning every pollutant into harmless food instantly
solution: Phytoremediation uses plants to help treat particular contamination. The pollutant, plant, and conditions determine whether it helps.
hint: The method concerns plant-assisted cleanup and has limits.

text: A treatment plant stores a pollutant in its tissues. What can be concluded from storage alone?
answers: The pollutant was taken up, but may not have been destroyed
Every pollutant at the site is now harmless
All polluted water is safe for drinking
The plant no longer needs photosynthesis
solution: Uptake and storage can move pollutants into plant tissues without destroying them. Storage alone does not prove site-wide safety.
hint: Distinguish moving a material from changing its identity.

text: Which record would best help evaluate a plant-based cleanup trial?
answers: Pollutant measurements using the same method over time
Leaf greenness alone, without pollutant measurements
Plant height alone, without testing the soil or water
Root length alone, without any before-treatment data
solution: Repeated pollutant measurements directly address whether contamination changes. Plant appearance or size alone does not show whether pollutants decreased.
hint: Choose a measurement of the outcome the trial is trying to change.

text: Two cleanup plots show lower pollution after rain, but only one has treatment plants. Why compare both plots?
answers: Rain or other shared conditions may explain some change
Comparison proves all plants work on all pollutants
The planted plot no longer needs measurements
The unplanted plot supplies light to the other
solution: A comparable untreated plot helps reveal changes due to rainfall or other shared factors. A decrease in one plot alone does not isolate the plant effect.
hint: Ask whether another condition could also change the measurement.

text: A notebook says, “The plants grew because they got bigger.” What is missing from the reasoning?
answers: A process linking growth to matter and energy inputs
The exact color of every plant container
A statement that soil supplies all new matter
A claim that sunlight is a mineral
solution: Scientific reasoning connects observations with a process. Air and water supply matter; photosynthesis uses light energy to make food for growth.
hint: Repeating the claim does not explain why it happened.

text: In a trial, soil-free seedlings developed new leaves. Which notebook sentence is evidence rather than a general claim or prediction?
answers: We recorded new leaves on the soil-free seedlings
All plants can grow under every condition
Our seedlings will probably grow tomorrow
Light is the material that becomes all leaves
solution: Evidence reports what was actually observed or measured. A broad claim or prediction is different from recorded trial results.
hint: Find the sentence that describes an observation.

text: A review sheet claims plants grow only in warm environments. Which correction is scientifically sound?
answers: Different plants can grow in different climates, including cold regions
Every plant grows equally well at every temperature
Temperature never affects plant growth
Cold places contain no plant life
solution: Plants are adapted to different environments, including cold ones. This corrects the warm-only claim without saying temperature never matters.
hint: Avoid replacing one absolute claim with another.

text: Which four-fact summary best connects the needs of a growing green plant?
answers: Air supplies carbon dioxide; roots absorb water; light supplies energy; sugar supports growth
Air supplies no matter; roots absorb light; soil is all food; leaves only decorate
Water supplies light; roots make air; sugar is a mineral; soil becomes all leaves
Air supplies sugar; water replaces light; roots absorb sunlight; leaves eat minerals
solution: A connected summary distinguishes matter inputs, plant structures, light energy, and food that supports growth. It should not call sunlight a material.
hint: Connect the source of matter with the source of energy and the food made.
